feedback: If the learner recomputes the subtraction from scratch, point back to the triangle: the whole (22) and two parts (15, 7) already give the subtraction — read it off rather than counting again.
If the learner writes 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, mark on the bar/triangle which number is the whole: you can only take a part away FROM the whole, and 15 and 7 are both parts.

If the learner checks 15 + 7 = 22 by just adding 15 + 7 again, point out that repeating the same calculation can repeat the same mistake. Reversing it (22 − 7 = 15) is a real check, in the same way that adding the parts back (15 + 7) checks the subtraction 22 − 7 = 15.
When the backward jump lands exactly on 15, name it: 'the subtraction undid the addition.'
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction reverses addition over the SAME three numbers, so taking one part from the whole returns the other part; one sum gives four related facts and a built-in way to check.
learnerActions: Start at 15 on a number line and make a forward jump of +7, landing on 22.
Before reversing, predict out loud where a backward jump of 7 will land and why.
Make the backward jump of −7 and confirm you return exactly to 15.
Say in your own words why the subtraction lands back on the start: it is the same jump run in reverse.
Fill in a fact-family triangle with the whole (22) and the two parts (15 and 7), then write all four facts: 15 + 7 = 22, 7 + 15 = 22, 22 − 7 = 15, 22 − 15 = 7.
Check a subtraction by adding the parts back: verify 22 − 7 = 15 by computing 15 + 7.

(Optional) Show the same reversing with another model: a balance that returns to its start after you add then subtract the same amount, or Cuisenaire rods laid as 15 + 7 and then the whole with one part removed.
activities.title: Do and undo it on a number line (with a fact-family triangle)

feedback: If the learner adds 9 and 14, remind them that the box plus 9 already makes 14, so you need to take 9 away from 14 to find the box.
Praise a correct check that substitutes the answer back into the original equation (5 + 9 = 14).
activities.intendedInsight: A missing-addend equation becomes a calculation you can already do by using the inverse operation, and the answer can be confirmed by reversing again.
learnerActions: Look at □ + 9 = 14 and decide what operation would find the missing part.
Explain why subtracting (14 − 9) finds the box: addition and subtraction undo each other.
Compute □ = 14 − 9 = 5 and check by putting it back: 5 + 9 = 14.
Try one or two more missing-number equations, each solved by the inverse and then checked by adding back.
activities.title: Solve a missing number by reversing

feedback: If the learner says 15 − 7 = 22, steer to the whole: 22 is the whole; you subtract a part from the whole, so valid subtractions are 22 − 7 and 22 − 15.
If the learner only recites facts without saying the operations undo each other, ask them to point to the jump that reverses the addition.
Accept a justification that names 22 as the whole and explains the returned part.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking works because addition reverses subtraction over the same whole and parts; the 'undo' idea applies to taking a part from the whole, not to any rearrangement of the three numbers.
learnerActions: Given 22 − 7 = 15, explain how you could be sure it is right WITHOUT redoing the subtraction.
Discuss the difference between reversing (adding the parts back) and simply repeating the same subtraction.
Respond to the claim that 'subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 = 22' and explain why that is wrong using which number is the whole.
State a DIFFERENT true subtraction from the same three numbers (22 − 15 = 7) and justify it.
activities.title: Explain WHY adding back proves a subtraction

feedback: For a choice that repeats 15 + 7, explain that a genuine check reverses the operation; an inverse check is 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 15 = 7).
For a mismatched subtraction, return to the whole-and-parts triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and recognition of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, reinforcing the single relationship.
learnerActions: Match one sum (15 + 7 = 22) to its three related facts.
Fill in blanks in missing-number equations such as □ + 9 = 14, solving by the inverse.
Choose which calculation correctly checks 15 + 7 = 22, distinguishing an inverse check (22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7) from a decoy that just repeats the same addition.
activities.title: Match and consolidate related facts
